cards.title: The GCP Resource Hierarchy
cards.teaser: GCP organizes everything into a four-level tree: Organization at the root, Folders for grouping, Projects as the unit of work, and individual Resources at the leaves. Every IAM policy and every billing charge attaches to a node in this tree.

runs.text: The resource hierarchy is not an administrative convenience — it is the structural backbone of GCP's security model. Policies set at a higher node flow downward to all children, and billing is aggregated upward through the same tree.

explanation.text:
Organization  (acme.com)
├── Folder: Production
│   ├── Project: prod-networking
│   ├── Project: prod-app
│   └── Project: prod-data
├── Folder: Staging
│   └── Project: staging-app
└── Folder: Shared
    └── Project: shared-services

items.text: — the root node, automatically created when a Google Workspace or Cloud Identity domain is linked to GCP. Every resource eventually lives under an org. Org admins hold the

— optional grouping layer between the org and projects. A folder can contain sub-folders and projects. Common patterns: one folder per business unit, per environment (prod/staging/dev), or per regulatory boundary.

— the fundamental unit of GCP work. Every resource (VM, bucket, database) lives inside a project. Projects have a unique numeric ID, a user-chosen project ID string, and a display name. Billing accounts attach at the project level.
— the leaves: Compute Engine instances, Cloud Storage buckets, BigQuery datasets, etc. Resources inherit the IAM policies of every ancestor node.

runs.text: Policy inheritance flows downward and is additive: a policy granted at the organization or folder level cannot be revoked by a child policy. If you grant a role at the org level, every project and resource in that org inherits it. Design your hierarchy before you deploy — reorganizing projects under different folders is possible but disruptive.

Think of GCP as a filing cabinet: the Organization is the cabinet, Folders are the drawers, Projects are the folders inside each drawer, and Resources are the individual documents. Any label you put on a drawer applies to everything inside it.

cards.title: Organization — Root of the Tree
cards.teaser: The Organization node is the top-level container for all GCP resources in a company. It is created automatically when a Google Workspace or Cloud Identity domain is associated with GCP, and it is where org-wide policies, billing, and admin roles live.

runs.text: An Organization resource has a one-to-one relationship with a Google Workspace or Cloud Identity domain. When your company's first GCP project is created by a user in that domain, GCP automatically provisions the Organization node.
Key characteristics:

items.text: Every project belongs to exactly one Organization. Projects without an org are personal projects (no org admins, no centralized governance).
The Organization ID is a stable numeric identifier. Use it in gcloud commands:
(manages the org resource and IAM policies on it) and
(manages Org Policy constraints). These are separate roles by design.
The Super Admin for the Google Workspace domain has special break-glass access to recover from misconfigured IAM at the org level.

explanation.text:
# List organizations your account can see
gcloud organizations list

# Describe a specific org
gcloud organizations describe 123456789012

# Get IAM policy at org level
gcloud organizations get-iam-policy 123456789012

runs.text: Never grant roles at the Organization level unless a principal genuinely needs access to all projects in the entire company. Org-level grants are inherited by every project — including ones created in the future.

The Organization is your company's GCP anchor. It ties your domain (acme.com) to all your cloud resources, gives org admins a centralized place to set guardrails, and is the root from which all IAM policies flow downward.

cards.title: Folders — Grouping Projects Under an Org
cards.teaser: Folders let you group projects into logical units — by team, environment, or regulatory boundary — and apply IAM policies and Org Policies to the group as a whole. They are optional but almost always worth using for anything beyond a handful of projects.

runs.text: A Folder sits between the Organization and Projects in the hierarchy. Folders can be nested up to 10 levels deep (in practice, 2-3 levels is common). A folder can contain other folders and projects.
Common folder patterns:

items.text: : Production / Staging / Development. Set tighter Org Policies and billing budgets on Production; allow looser constraints in Development.
: Engineering / Finance / Marketing. Each unit gets its own billing account and IAM boundary.
: PCI-scoped folder with restricted regions; HIPAA folder with additional Org Policy constraints. Auditors can review the folder and its children as a unit.

explanation.text:
# Create a folder under the organization
gcloud resource-manager folders create \
  --display-name="Production" \
  --organization=123456789012

# Create a sub-folder under a folder
gcloud resource-manager folders create \
  --display-name="PCI" \
  --folder=PARENT_FOLDER_ID

# List folders in an organization
gcloud resource-manager folders list --organization=123456789012

runs.text: IAM policies set on a Folder are inherited by all projects and resources inside it. This is the primary reason to use Folders: instead of granting a role on 20 projects one-by-one, grant it once on the parent Folder.

Folders are drawers in your filing cabinet — they let you group related projects together and apply the same policies to all of them at once, without repeating yourself across every individual project.

cards.title: Project — The Unit of GCP Work
cards.teaser: Every GCP resource lives inside a project. The project is simultaneously the billing boundary, the API-enablement boundary, the IAM boundary, and the quota boundary. Understanding project design is the prerequisite for everything else in GCP.

runs.text: A Project has three identifiers:

items.text: ). Immutable after creation. Used in API calls,
— automatically assigned numeric ID. Used internally by GCP APIs. Cannot be changed.

explanation.text:
# Create a new project inside a folder
gcloud projects create acme-prod-app-2024 \
  --name="Acme Production App" \
  --folder=FOLDER_ID

# Link a billing account
gcloud billing projects link acme-prod-app-2024 \
  --billing-account=01A2B3-C4D5E6-F7G8H9

# Enable an API in the project
gcloud services enable compute.googleapis.com \
  --project=acme-prod-app-2024

# Set default project in gcloud config
gcloud config set project acme-prod-app-2024

runs.text: Design implications: one project per environment per application is the standard pattern. Sharing a project between prod and staging is a common early shortcut that leads to billing confusion and IAM complexity. Each project requires an explicitly enabled billing account; resources cannot be created in a project with no billing account (except free-tier quotas).

Deleting a project schedules it for deletion after 30 days. During that window all APIs are disabled and resources stop running, but the project still consumes quota. Use gcloud projects undelete PROJECT_ID within 30 days to recover it.

A project is your unit of work in GCP — it is where you deploy resources, where you pay, where you control access, and where you set API permissions. Think of it as one application environment's private walled garden.

cards.title: IAM Principals — Who Can Act
cards.teaser: An IAM principal identifies who is making a request. GCP recognizes six principal types: Google Accounts, service accounts, Google Groups, Google Workspace domains, Cloud Identity domains, and the special identifiers allUsers and allAuthenticatedUsers.

runs.text: Every IAM policy binding pairs a principal with a role. Understanding principal types is the first step to writing secure policies.

items.text: — a specific Google Account (personal Gmail or Workspace account).
— a Google Group. Preferred for human access: manage group membership in Google Admin; IAM policies stay stable.
— a non-human identity for workloads, VMs, and applications.
— every user in a Google Workspace or Cloud Identity domain. Use with care: grants access to all present and future domain members.
— any user authenticated with a Google Account. Not recommended for sensitive resources.
— literally everyone on the internet, including unauthenticated callers. Only appropriate for public websites and open data buckets.

runs.text: Best practice: manage human access through Google Groups, not individual user: bindings. When an engineer joins or leaves a team, update group membership in one place instead of updating IAM policies across multiple projects.
GCP also supports
principal sets
via Workload Identity Federation: external identities from AWS, GitHub Actions, Azure, or any OIDC/SAML provider are mapped to a principal of the form
principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/POOL_ID/attribute.repository/REPO

A principal is the "who" in an IAM policy: it can be a person, a group of people, an application, or even the open internet. Every grant in GCP names a principal and says what that principal is allowed to do.

cards.title: IAM Roles — Primitive, Predefined, and Custom
cards.teaser: GCP bundles permissions into roles. There are three role types: primitive roles (coarse, legacy), predefined roles (purpose-built per service, the right default), and custom roles (hand-crafted for least privilege when predefined roles are too broad).

runs.text: A role is a named collection of permissions. You never grant individual permissions in a policy — you grant a role, and the role carries the permissions.

items.text: — three roles that predate GCP IAM:
. They grant broad, cross-service access (Owner includes everything Editor does plus billing and IAM management). Avoid them in production; prefer predefined roles.
— curated by Google, one per service/function (e.g.,
). Updated by Google as services evolve. The right choice for most workloads.

— you define the exact permission set. Required when a predefined role grants more access than the principal needs. Defined at org or project level; not automatically updated when GCP adds new permissions to a service.

explanation.text:
# List all predefined roles for Cloud Storage
gcloud iam roles list --filter="name:roles/storage"

# Describe a predefined role's permissions
gcloud iam roles describe roles/storage.objectViewer

# Create a custom role at project level
gcloud iam roles create invoker \
  --project=my-project \
  --title="Custom Cloud Run Invoker" \
  --description="Invoke Cloud Run services only" \
  --permissions=run.routes.invoke \
  --stage=GA

runs.text: Primitive roles are still in wide use but violate the principle of least privilege at scale. Granting roles/editor to a service account gives it the ability to delete databases, modify network configs, and read secrets across the entire project. Use predefined or custom roles for all non-trivial principals.

Primitive roles are the sledgehammer — broad and blunt. Predefined roles are purpose-built tools — one per job. Custom roles are the precision instruments you craft when even the purpose-built tools give too much access.

cards.title: IAM Policy Bindings and Inheritance
cards.teaser: An IAM policy is a collection of bindings. Each binding pairs a role with one or more principals. Policies attach to resources at every level of the hierarchy, and child resources inherit the union of all ancestor policies — grants are additive, never subtractive.

runs.text: An IAM policy document in GCP looks like this:

explanation.text:
# IAM policy YAML for a project
bindings:
  - role: roles/bigquery.dataViewer
    members:
      - group:analysts@acme.com
      - user:contractor@partner.com
  - role: roles/bigquery.jobUser
    members:
      - group:analysts@acme.com
  - role: roles/storage.objectViewer
    members:
      - serviceAccount:etl-runner@acme-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com
etag: BwXxYzZz123=
version: 3

runs.text: Inheritance rules:

items.text: A policy at the Organization level applies to all Folders, Projects, and Resources inside it.
A policy at a Folder applies to all Projects and Resources inside that Folder.
A policy at a Project applies to all Resources inside that Project.

The effective policy for a resource is the union of all policies from all ancestor nodes. You cannot use a child policy to deny access granted by a parent — use IAM deny policies (GA as of 2023) for that.

explanation.text:
# Grant a role on a project
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding my-project \
  --member="user:alice@example.com" \
  --role="roles/bigquery.dataViewer"

# Get the full policy of a project
gcloud projects get-iam-policy my-project --format=yaml

# Grant a role on a specific bucket (resource-level policy)
gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding gs://my-bucket \
  --member="group:readers@example.com" \
  --role="roles/storage.objectViewer"

runs.text: An IAM policy is a list of who-gets-what. Policies stack downward: if your org policy says Alice is a viewer, and your project policy also says Alice is an editor, Alice ends up with both — the most permissive union of all parent and child policies.

cards.title: IAM Conditions — Attribute-Based Access Control
cards.teaser: IAM Conditions let you add logic to a policy binding: grant a role only during business hours, only for resources with a specific tag, only when the request originates from a trusted network. Conditions turn coarse bindings into fine-grained access control.

runs.text: An IAM Condition is a CEL (Common Expression Language) expression attached to a role binding. The binding is only effective when the condition evaluates to true.
Three categories of condition attributes:

items.text: . Scope a grant to specific buckets, VMs, or services.
. Grant access only during a time window (temporary access, contractor with an expiry date, maintenance windows).

explanation.text:
# Grant Storage Object Viewer only for objects with a specific prefix
gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding gs://my-bucket \
  --member="serviceAccount:consumer@proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \
  --role="roles/storage.objectViewer" \
  --condition='expression=resource.name.startsWith("projects/_/buckets/my-bucket/objects/reports/"),title=reports-only'

# Grant a role that expires on 2026-12-31
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding my-project \
  --member="user:contractor@example.com" \
  --role="roles/viewer" \
  --condition='expression=request.time < timestamp("2026-12-31T00:00:00Z"),title=temp-contractor-access'

runs.text: Conditions require IAM policy version 3. When you add a condition to any binding in a policy, you must set the policy version field to 3, or the condition will be silently ignored during evaluation.

IAM Conditions are the "but only if" clause in a permission grant. Instead of "Alice can read this bucket," you say "Alice can read this bucket, but only before December 31 and only for files starting with /reports/." The logic is a small expression evaluated at request time.

cards.title: Service Accounts — Non-Human Identities for Workloads
cards.teaser: A service account is a special Google Account used by applications, VMs, and workloads — not by humans. Instead of sharing a developer's credentials in code, you bind a service account to the workload and grant only the permissions that workload needs.

runs.text: Service accounts serve a dual role in GCP: they are both an
identity
(like a user, they can be granted IAM roles) and a
resource
(they can have their own IAM policy controlling who can use them). This duality is a common source of confusion.

items.text: — GCP automatically creates service accounts for Compute Engine and App Engine. These default accounts come with the Editor primitive role, which is overly permissive. Always disable or restrict default service accounts.
— you create these explicitly and grant only the minimum roles required. One service account per workload or microservice is the standard pattern.
role on a service account, and they can generate short-lived tokens for that account without needing a key file.

explanation.text:
# Create a service account
gcloud iam service-accounts create etl-runner \
  --display-name="ETL Pipeline Runner" \
  --project=my-project

# Grant the SA roles on a resource
gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding gs://my-data-bucket \
  --member="serviceAccount:etl-runner@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \
  --role="roles/storage.objectAdmin"

# Attach a service account to a Compute Engine VM
gcloud compute instances create my-vm \
  --service-account=etl-runner@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --scopes=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform

runs.text: GCP's metadata server provides short-lived credentials to VMs automatically — code running on a VM with an attached service account does not need to handle credentials at all. The Application Default Credentials (ADC) library discovers the metadata server transparently.

A service account is the identity badge for an application. Instead of putting your personal credentials in code, you create a dedicated badge for the app, grant that badge only what it needs, and attach it to the workload. GCP handles the rest.

cards.title: Service Account Keys — The Anti-Pattern to Avoid
cards.teaser: Service account keys are long-lived JSON credentials that can authenticate as a service account from anywhere. They are convenient and dangerous: lost keys grant indefinite access with no automatic expiry. Use them only when there is no better option.

runs.text: When you create a service account key, GCP generates an RSA key pair: you download the private key as a JSON file, and GCP stores the public key. The private key allows anyone in possession of it to authenticate as the service account — from any machine, forever, until the key is deleted.
Why keys are an anti-pattern:

items.text: They are long-lived. Unlike short-lived OAuth tokens (1 hour), a service account key does not expire unless you rotate it manually.
They are easily leaked. Keys end up in Git repos, Docker images, CI logs, and Slack messages. The GCP Security Command Center surfaces keys detected in public repositories.
They bypass audit: if a key is stolen, an attacker can act as the service account from outside GCP with no VPC Service Controls or Access Context Manager rules applying.

explanation.text:
# Create a key (avoid in favor of Workload Identity or impersonation)
gcloud iam service-accounts keys create key.json \
  --iam-account=my-sa@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com

# List all keys for a service account
gcloud iam service-accounts keys list \
  --iam-account=my-sa@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com

# Delete a compromised or unused key
gcloud iam service-accounts keys delete KEY_ID \
  --iam-account=my-sa@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com

# Org Policy to disable key creation across the org
# constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation

runs.text: Google's own recommendation is to disable service account key creation at the org level using the Org Policy constraint iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation, and use Workload Identity Federation for any external workload that needs GCP access. Keys should be the exception, not the default.

A service account key is a master key that never changes and can be used from anywhere. That makes it extremely convenient and extremely dangerous. Modern GCP deployments replace keys with short-lived federated tokens wherever possible.

cards.title: Workload Identity Federation — Keyless Auth for External Workloads
cards.teaser: Workload Identity Federation lets workloads running outside GCP (on AWS, Azure, GitHub Actions, on-premises Kubernetes) authenticate using their existing identity tokens — no service account key file required. It is the modern replacement for downloaded keys.

runs.text: The core idea: external platforms already issue short-lived identity tokens (AWS instance identity documents, GitHub Actions OIDC tokens, Kubernetes service account tokens). Workload Identity Federation teaches GCP to trust those tokens, so an external workload can exchange its native token for a short-lived GCP access token.
The setup has three parts:

items.text: — a container for external identity providers. You create one pool per trust boundary (e.g., one pool for GitHub Actions, one for AWS).
— defines the external IdP (GitHub Actions OIDC, AWS STS, Azure AD, or any OIDC/SAML provider) and the attribute mapping (which fields of the external token map to GCP principal attributes).
— grants a role to a principal set from the pool, optionally scoped to specific attribute values (e.g., only tokens where the GitHub repo is

explanation.text:
# 1. Create a Workload Identity Pool
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools create github-pool \
  --location="global" \
  --display-name="GitHub Actions Pool"

# 2. Add GitHub Actions as an OIDC provider
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers create-oidc github-provider \
  --location="global" \
  --workload-identity-pool="github-pool" \
  --issuer-uri="https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com" \
  --attribute-mapping="google.subject=assertion.sub,attribute.repository=assertion.repository"

# 3. Grant the pool access to a service account, scoped to a specific repo
POOL="projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/github-pool"
gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding deploy-sa@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --role="roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser" \
  --member="principalSet://${POOL}/attribute.repository/my-org/my-repo"

runs.text: In a GitHub Actions workflow, the workload calls the GCP STS endpoint with its OIDC token, receives a short-lived GCP access token, and uses it directly — no JSON key file is ever created or stored.

Workload Identity Federation is also the mechanism behind GKE Workload Identity: pods are mapped to service accounts via a pool provider that trusts the GKE cluster's Kubernetes API, eliminating the need to mount service account key secrets into pods.

Workload Identity Federation is a trust agreement: "I, GCP, agree to accept tokens issued by GitHub (or AWS, or your Kubernetes cluster). When you show me one of those tokens, I will give you a short-lived GCP credential that expires in an hour." No static keys need to exist anywhere.

cards.title: Org Policies — Guardrails Across the Hierarchy
cards.teaser: Organization Policies let admins enforce company-wide constraints on what GCP resources can be configured — disable external IPs on VMs, restrict Cloud Run to internal ingress only, prevent public Cloud Storage buckets. They enforce intent, not just access.

runs.text: IAM answers "who can do what." Org Policies answer "what configurations are allowed to exist at all." Even if a principal has the permission to configure external IPs, an Org Policy constraint can prevent the configuration from being set.
Key Org Policy concepts:

items.text: — the rules available to enforce. GCP provides 100+ managed constraints. Examples:
(restrict which regions resources can be created in).
— how you apply a constraint at a specific node. You set a policy to Enforce (boolean constraints) or define an allowed/denied values list (list constraints).
— like IAM, Org Policies inherit downward. A policy set at the org level applies to all folders and projects. Child nodes can override parent policies only if the policy allows it (the

explanation.text:
# Enforce "no external IPs" on all VMs in the org
gcloud resource-manager org-policies set-policy \
  --organization=123456789012 \
  /dev/stdin <<EOF
constraint: constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess
booleanPolicy:
  enforced: true
EOF

# Restrict resource creation to US regions only
gcloud resource-manager org-policies set-policy \
  --folder=FOLDER_ID \
  /dev/stdin <<EOF
constraint: constraints/gcp.resourceLocations
listPolicy:
  allowedValues:
    - in:us-locations
EOF

# Describe an org policy at a project level
gcloud resource-manager org-policies describe \
  constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess \
  --project=my-project

runs.text: Org Policies and IAM are complementary. Use IAM to control who can act. Use Org Policies to enforce what configurations are permissible. A strong security baseline uses both: IAM prevents unauthorized API calls; Org Policies prevent misconfigurations even by authorized users.

Org Policies are the company rulebook. IAM says who is allowed to do things; Org Policies say what things are allowed to exist. Even if your CTO has full project owner rights, an Org Policy can still prevent them from creating a VM with a public IP address.

cards.title: Cloud Audit Logs — The Immutable Record of Who Did What
cards.teaser: Cloud Audit Logs automatically record every admin action, data access, and system event on GCP resources. They are the cornerstone of compliance, incident response, and security investigation — and unlike application logs, they cannot be disabled for admin activity.

runs.text: Cloud Audit Logs captures three categories of events:

items.text: — every write operation on resource metadata: creating a VM, changing an IAM policy, deleting a bucket. Always enabled, free, 400-day retention. Cannot be disabled.

— read and write operations on resource data: reading a BigQuery table, reading Cloud Storage objects, reading Secret Manager secrets. Disabled by default (high volume, incurs cost). Must be explicitly enabled per service.
— GCP internal operations (live migration of a VM, auto-scaling events). Always enabled, free.

runs.text: Each log entry includes:

items.text: The principal (who) — the authenticated identity that made the call.
The method (what) — the exact API method invoked (e.g.,
The resource (on what) — the full resource name.
The timestamp, status (success/failure), and the caller's IP address.

explanation.text:
# Query admin activity logs for IAM policy changes in the last 24h
gcloud logging read \
  'logName="projects/my-project/logs/cloudaudit.googleapis.com%2Factivity" \
   protoPayload.methodName="SetIamPolicy"' \
  --freshness=24h \
  --format=json

# Enable Data Access logs for Cloud Storage (via IAM audit config)
# Set in the project IAM policy:
# auditConfigs:
#   - auditLogConfigs:
#     - logType: DATA_READ
#     - logType: DATA_WRITE
#     service: storage.googleapis.com

# Export audit logs to BigQuery via a log sink
gcloud logging sinks create audit-to-bq \
  bigquery.googleapis.com/projects/my-project/datasets/audit_logs \
  --log-filter='logName:(cloudaudit.googleapis.com)' \
  --project=my-project

runs.text: For compliance frameworks (PCI DSS, HIPAA, SOC 2), export audit logs to a separate, locked-down project via a Log Sink to a Cloud Storage bucket with object retention locks. This ensures audit logs cannot be tampered with even by project owners of the source project.

Cloud Audit Logs are GCP's security camera system. Admin Activity logs automatically record every configuration change — who moved what furniture. Data Access logs record who read or wrote to your data. You cannot turn off the admin camera, which is exactly the point.
